senses.gloss:
kirāta
(‘hunter’)
------------------------------------------
Though the चस्ते स्य्स्तेम् has no direct connection with Hindu religion or philosophies as such, the caste factor has often proved to be an irritation to the body of the Hindu society.
Of the several castes assigned to the category of शूद्रस् or even to that of the caṇḍālas, the kirātas are also one group. If मनु (Manusmṛti 10.43 & 44) considers them as originally kṣattriyas reduced to the status of शूद्रस् due to the non-performance of their religious duties, the Vedavyāsasmṛti (1.10 & 11) considers them as a subdivision of शूद्रस्. Others assign them to the group of म्लेच्छस् (untouchable foreigners)!
They live in forests by hunting wild animals and are fiery fighters.
When अर्जुन was performing severe austerities to get the grace of शिव, the latter is said to have tested his valour by appearing before him in the guise of a किरात.

kirīṭa
(‘that by which [fame] spreads’, ‘crown’)
------------------------------------------
Hindu gods and goddesses as also emperors and kings are always shown with a किरीट (also called makuṭa or मुकुट) on their heads. It is the crown.
A किरीट is usually tall and tapering. It generally has three parts: the paṭṭa (the band, the lowest part); the gātra (main body, bedecked with gems) and the śikhāmaṇi (crest-jewel).
The किरीट may be plain (like a conical cap) or decorated with precious stones. The top is generally dome-shaped surmounted by a jewel called ‘śikhāmaṇi’.
A किरीट is sometimes called ‘kirīṭa-मुकुट’ to distinguish it from ‘jaṭāmukuṭa’ (hair dressed as a crown).

kīrtana
(‘praising’)
------------------------------------------
The भक्ति-movements of the middle ages, pioneered and developed by a galaxy of poet-mystics and mystical philosophers, made religion very easy of access to the masses. They laid great stress on nāmajapa (repetition of the divine name or मन्त्र) and कीर्तन (singing the names and glories of God) and taught that these two were enough to wash off one’s sins and obtain the grace of God.
Kīrtana is singing the names of the Divine or devotional songs, generally to the accompaniment of musical instruments. Group-singing is sometimes called ‘saṅkīrtana’.
There may also be dancing to the tune and rhythm of the songs.
Kīrtana is also the name of a work by the great mystic and religious teacher of Assam, शङ्कर Deva (A. D. 1486-1568), in simple verses suited to मुसिच् and depicting the story of Lord कृष्ण as in the Bhāgavata.

kīrtimukha
(‘face of glory’)
------------------------------------------
In almost all हिन्दु तेम्प्लेस्, behind the main image, there is an ornamental arch, generally called ‘prabhāvalī’ or ‘prabhāmaṇḍala’. The use of such prabhā-valīs dates back to the second century A. D. The central part of the top portion has the head of a leonine figure with protruding eyes, open mouth and fierce fangs. The tongue is lolling out. This figure is called ‘kīrtimukha’ or the ‘face of glory’.
As per the story in the Padmapurāṇa, Jālandhara, a fierce demon, fell in love with पार्वती and sent राहु (See RĀHU.) to शिव demanding that he part with her. Enraged by this indecent demand, शिव created a terrible being from his hair and commanded it to swallow राहु. When राहु pleaded for mercy, his life was saved but the being created wanted something else to appease his hunger. शिव asked him to devour his own body! Since the latter could devour his whole body except his own head, शिव being pleased with his implicit obedience blessed him that his bodiless head would hereafter, be represented in all temples and worship offered to it along with the icon.
